title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (RFC 2119)
evaluation_goals: Assess whether the document clearly, unambiguously, and concisely defines normative requirement levels for IETF specifications, provides exact operational definitions of keywords, prevents misinterpretation, and includes necessary security considerations.
overall_assessment: RFC 2119 is one of the most foundational, high-quality, and influential technical specifications in Internet history. It achieves near-perfection in brevity, clarity, and normative rigor.

criteria.name: Normative Keyword Definition Precision
criteria.description: Exhaustive and unambiguous operational definitions of MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, OPTIONAL.
criteria.scoring_guidance: Full marks (7.0-8.0): Definitions distinguish absolute necessity from recommendation and explain interoperability risks. Partial (4.0-6.5): Defines major keywords but lacks clarity on subtle distinctions. Zero (0.0-3.5): Ambiguous, self-contradictory definitions or missing keywords.
criteria.justification: Lines 31-72 provide precise, operational definitions for all 10 keywords. For example, L31-32: "1. MUST This word, or the terms 'REQUIRED' or 'SHALL', mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification." And L43-46 for SHOULD: "there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course."

criteria.name: Standard Boilerplate Specification
criteria.description: Provides explicit boilerplate text that authors must incorporate near the beginning of documents to invoke the standard.
criteria.scoring_guidance: Full marks (4.5-5.0): Exact, copy-pasteable boilerplate phrase and clear location instructions. Partial (2.5-4.0): Mentions boilerplate without exact phrasing. Zero (0.0-2.0): Omits boilerplate instruction entirely.
criteria.justification: Lines 20-26 explicitly instruct: "Authors who follow these guidelines should incorporate this phrase near the beginning of their document: The key words 'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', 'MAY', and 'OPTIONAL' in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119."

criteria.name: Guidance on Proper Imperative Usage and Restraint
criteria.description: Explicitly cautions against overuse of imperative keywords and explains they must only be used where required for interoperability.
criteria.scoring_guidance: Full marks (6.0-7.0): Explicitly warns against overuse and explains interoperability requirements. Partial (3.0-5.5): Advises care in usage but lacks specific guidance on interoperability relevance. Zero (0.0-2.5): Encourages unconstrained usage.
criteria.justification: Lines 74-95 (Section 6 "Guidance in the use of these Imperatives") state: "Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm...". Deducted 0.5 because concrete examples of borderline misuse in actual RFC protocols could have further clarified edge cases.

criteria.name: Security Considerations for Protocol Requirements
criteria.description: Details security ramifications of non-compliance, particularly how ignoring MUST/SHOULD recommendations can create security vulnerabilities.
criteria.scoring_guidance: Full marks (4.5-5.0): Details security ramifications of non-compliance. Partial (2.5-4.0): Mentions security generally. Zero (0.0-2.0): Omits security considerations entirely.
criteria.justification: Lines 97-104 (Section 7 "Security Considerations") state: "These terms are frequently used to specify behavior with security implications. The effects on security of not implementing a MUST or a SHOULD, or doing something the procedure says MUST NOT or SHOULD NOT be done may be very subtle." Deducted 0.5 because the section is brief without concrete illustrative security failure modes.
